arXiv:2604.12811v1 [cs.LG] 14 Apr 2026

Algorithmic Analysis of Dense Associative Memory:
Finite-Size Guarantees and Adversarial Robustness

Madhava Gaikwad Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: gaikwad.madhav@gmail.com
Abstract

Dense Associative Memory (DAM) generalizes Hopfield networks through higher-order interactions and achieves storage capacity that scales as O⁡(Nn−1)O(N^{n-1}) under suitable pattern separation conditions. Existing dynamical analyses primarily study the thermodynamic limit N→∞N\to\infty with randomly sampled patterns and therefore do not provide finite-size guarantees or explicit convergence rates.

We develop an algorithmic analysis of DAM retrieval dynamics that yields finite-NN guarantees under explicit, verifiable pattern conditions. Under a separation assumption and a bounded-interference condition at high loading, we prove geometric convergence of asynchronous retrieval dynamics, which implies O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) convergence time once the trajectory enters the basin of attraction. We further establish adversarial robustness bounds expressed through an explicit margin condition that quantifies the number of corrupted bits tolerable per sweep, and derive capacity guarantees that scale as Θ⁡(Nn−1)\Theta(N^{n-1}) up to polylogarithmic factors in the worst case, while recovering the classical Θ⁡(Nn−1)\Theta(N^{n-1}) scaling for random pattern ensembles. Finally, we show that DAM retrieval dynamics admit a potential-game interpretation that ensures convergence to pure Nash equilibria under asynchronous updates.

Complete proofs are provided in the appendices, together with preliminary experiments that illustrate the predicted convergence, robustness, and capacity scaling behavior.

1 Introduction

Dense Associative Memory (DAM) stores pp binary patterns {𝝃μ}μ=1p⊂{−1,+1}N\{\bm{\xi}^{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{p}\subset\{-1,+1\}^{N} in an NN-neuron network through higher-order interactions Krotov & Hopfield (2016). For interaction order n≥2n\geq 2, the energy function is

E(𝒙)=−1Nn−1∑μ=1p(∑i=1Nξiμxi)n,E(\bm{x})=-\frac{1}{N^{n-1}}\sum_{\mu=1}^{p}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\xi_{i}^{\mu}x_{i}\right)^{n}, (1)

with local field hi​(𝒙)=∂(−E)/∂xih_{i}(\bm{x})=\partial(-E)/\partial x_{i} and asynchronous update rule

xi←sign⁡(hi​(𝒙)).x_{i}\leftarrow\operatorname{sign}(h_{i}(\bm{x})).

Classical statistical-physics analyses of associative memory models focus primarily on asymptotic behavior in the thermodynamic limit and typically assume randomly sampled patterns. Recent work by Mimura et al. Mimura et al. (2025) provides an asymptotically exact dynamical analysis of DAM using generating functional analysis (GFA). Their results apply to the regime N→∞N\to\infty with random i.i.d. patterns and show that for interaction orders n≥3n\geq 3 the effective noise variance becomes independent of the overlap, which mitigates a key instability present in classical Hopfield networks (n=2n=2). However, this framework does not provide explicit finite-NN convergence guarantees, does not address adversarial or structured pattern sets, and does not yield explicit retrieval-time bounds.

This work develops an algorithmic analysis that complements the statistical-physics perspective by focusing on finite systems and explicit performance guarantees. We introduce explicit separation and bounded-interference assumptions on the stored patterns that can be verified directly or shown to hold with high probability for random ensembles. Under these conditions we obtain finite-size convergence guarantees, robustness bounds under adversarial corruption, and explicit capacity guarantees that recover the classical Nn−1N^{n-1} scaling up to polylogarithmic factors in the worst case.

Appendix A contains complete proofs of the main results, including the strengthened interference condition required near capacity loading, the potential-game characterization of retrieval dynamics, and verification that random pattern ensembles satisfy the assumptions with high probability. Appendix B reports preliminary experiments on a cubic (n=3n=3) DAM that illustrate convergence behavior, basin-of-attraction structure, adversarial robustness thresholds, capacity scaling, comparisons between synchronous and asynchronous updates, and retrieval performance on binarized MNIST and CIFAR-10 data.

2 Related Work

The foundational work of Hopfield (1982) established recurrent neural networks as physical systems with emergent computational abilities, a perspective deeply analyzed using spin-glass theory Amit et al. (1985), Amit (1989). The theoretical storage capacity of these classical models was rigorously quantified in seminal works Newman (1988), Gardner (1987), McEliece et al. (1987), Abbott & Arian (1987). A major leap forward was the introduction of Dense Associative Memory (DAM) models Krotov & Hopfield (2016), which achieve exponential storage capacity Lucibello & Mézard (2024) and have been shown to be practically powerful in deep learning architectures Ramsauer et al. (2021), Hoover et al. (2023). Recent theoretical advances have further explored the dynamical properties Mimura et al. (2025), saddle point hierarchies Thériault & Tantari (2026), and biological plausibility of these modern networks Kafraj et al. (2026). This resurgence has also led to novel applications in analog circuits Bacvanski et al. (2025), optical computing Musa et al. (2026), and as a framework for understanding Transformer architectures Masumura & Taki (2025). The field’s enduring relevance is underscored by recent surveys and tutorials at major AI conferences Krotov et al. (2025), Kempe et al. (2024) and its connection to broader topics in optimization Boyd & Vandenberghe (2004), Shalev-Shwartz & Ben-David (2014), Goles & Martínez (1985), game theory Monderer & Shapley (1996), Hart & Mas-Colell (2003), and robust machine learning Cohen et al. (2019), Ge et al. (2015), Du et al. (2019).

3 Problem Formulation

3.1 Model and Updates

We analyze asynchronous updates, where at each iteration a single neuron is selected uniformly at random and updated according to

xi(t+1)=sign⁡(hi​(𝒙(t)))for randomly selected ​i.x_{i}^{(t+1)}=\operatorname{sign}\!\left(h_{i}(\bm{x}^{(t)})\right)\quad\text{for randomly selected }i. (2)

Asynchronous updates ensure monotone improvement of the energy function and avoid oscillatory behaviors that may arise under synchronous updates in Hopfield-type networks Goles & Martínez (1985).

We measure time in full sweeps, where one sweep corresponds to NN consecutive asynchronous updates so that, in expectation, each neuron is updated once.

For a stored pattern 𝝃ν\bm{\xi}^{\nu}, the overlap of a state 𝒙\bm{x} with the target pattern is

mν​(𝒙)=1N​∑i=1Nξiν​xi.m^{\nu}(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\xi_{i}^{\nu}x_{i}.

3.2 Pattern Separation

To obtain finite-size guarantees, we impose a separation condition that characterizes the basin of attraction of a stored pattern.

Assumption 1 (Pattern Separation).

Fix a target pattern ν\nu. There exist constants γ>0\gamma>0 and β<γ\beta<\gamma such that for all states 𝐱\bm{x} satisfying

mν​(𝒙)≥γ,m^{\nu}(\bm{x})\geq\gamma,

the interference from all non-target patterns is bounded as

maxμ≠ν⁡|1N​∑i=1Nξiμ​xi|≤β.\max_{\mu\neq\nu}\left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\xi_{i}^{\mu}x_{i}\right|\leq\beta.

This condition requires that once the trajectory enters a basin of attraction characterized by overlap at least γ\gamma, the contribution of every competing pattern remains strictly smaller than that of the target pattern. For random i.i.d. patterns, the condition holds with high probability when the loading satisfies p=o⁡(Nn−1)p=o(N^{n-1}), while the subsequent analysis applies to any deterministic pattern set that satisfies the assumption.

4 Main Results

Theorem 2 (Convergence Rate).

Suppose the stored patterns satisfy Assumption 1 with γ>β\gamma>\beta, and let the loading satisfy p≤Nn−12​n​(n−1)p\leq\frac{N^{n-1}}{2n(n-1)}. Then asynchronous DAM retrieval initialized at any state with mν​(𝐱(0))≥γm^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(0)})\geq\gamma converges to the target pattern in

T=O⁡(1α​log⁡N)T=O\!\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\log N\right)

full sweeps, where

α=1n−2​(n−1)​pNn−1>0.\alpha=\frac{1}{n}-\frac{2(n-1)p}{N^{n-1}}>0.
Theorem 3 (Adversarial Robustness).

Under the conditions of Theorem 2, retrieval succeeds despite adversarial corruption of up to ρ​N\rho N bits per full sweep provided

ρ<α2.\rho<\frac{\alpha}{2}.

In particular, using the explicit expression for α\alpha yields the bound

ρ<12​(1n−2​(n−1)​pNn−1).\rho<\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{n}-\frac{2(n-1)p}{N^{n-1}}\right).
Theorem 4 (Capacity Scaling).

Assume the pattern set satisfies Assumption 1. Then DAM retrieval guarantees hold for at least

p≥Nn−14​n2​(n−1)2p\geq\frac{N^{n-1}}{4n^{2}(n-1)^{2}}

stored patterns, while retrieval may fail when the loading becomes p=Ω⁡(Nn−1)p=\Omega(N^{n-1}). Thus the achievable storage capacity scales as Θ⁡(Nn−1)\Theta(N^{n-1}) up to constant or polylogarithmic factors depending on the pattern ensemble.

Theorem 5 (Game-Theoretic Characterization).

DAM asynchronous dynamics coincide with best-response dynamics in an exact potential game with

  • •

    players: neurons i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N,

  • •

    actions: xi∈{−1,+1}x_{i}\in\{-1,+1\},

  • •

    payoffs: ui​(𝒙)=xi​hi​(𝒙)u_{i}(\bm{x})=x_{i}h_{i}(\bm{x}),

  • •

    potential: F⁡(𝒙)=−E⁡(𝒙)F(\bm{x})=-E(\bm{x}).

All limit points of the dynamics are pure Nash equilibria.

5 Analytical Framework

5.1 Coordinate-Descent View

DAM asynchronous updates perform coordinate ascent on the potential F⁡(𝒙)=−E⁡(𝒙)F(\bm{x})=-E(\bm{x}).

Lemma 6 (Potential Improvement).

Let coordinate ii be updated asynchronously according to xi(t+1)=sign⁡(hi​(𝐱(t)))x_{i}^{(t+1)}=\operatorname{sign}(h_{i}(\bm{x}^{(t)})). Then

F⁡(𝒙(t+1))−F⁡(𝒙(t))=2​|ϕi​(𝒙−i(t))|,F(\bm{x}^{(t+1)})-F(\bm{x}^{(t)})=2\,|\phi_{i}(\bm{x}^{(t)}_{-i})|,

where

ϕi​(𝒙−i)=12​(F⁡(+1,𝒙−i)−F⁡(−1,𝒙−i)).\phi_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i})=\frac{1}{2}\left(F(+1,\bm{x}_{-i})-F(-1,\bm{x}_{-i})\right).

Under Assumption 1 inside the basin mν​(𝐱)≥γm^{\nu}(\bm{x})\geq\gamma, each misaligned coordinate satisfies |ϕi|≥c⁡(γ,β,n)>0|\phi_{i}|\geq c(\gamma,\beta,n)>0, implying strict potential improvement whenever an incorrect neuron is updated.

5.2 Contraction Analysis

Lemma 7 (Overlap Contraction).

Under the loading condition p≤Nn−12​n​(n−1)p\leq\frac{N^{n-1}}{2n(n-1)} and Assumption 1, the asynchronous dynamics satisfy

𝔼⁡[mν​(𝒙(t+1))]≥mν​(𝒙(t))+αN​(1−mν​(𝒙(t))),\mathbb{E}[m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t+1)})]\geq m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t)})+\frac{\alpha}{N}\left(1-m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t)})\right),

where

α=1n−2​(n−1)​pNn−1>0.\alpha=\frac{1}{n}-\frac{2(n-1)p}{N^{n-1}}>0.
Proof sketch.

The local field decomposes as

hi​(𝒙)=n​ξiν​(mν)n−1+ηi,h_{i}(\bm{x})=n\xi_{i}^{\nu}(m^{\nu})^{n-1}+\eta_{i},

where ηi\eta_{i} represents interference from non-target patterns. Assumption 1 ensures the signal term dominates the interference inside the basin, so that each misaligned neuron updates correctly with probability at least α\alpha. Averaging over random coordinate selection yields the stated expected improvement. ∎

5.3 Adversarial Analysis

Proof sketch of Theorem 3.

Let ℳ(t)\mathcal{M}^{(t)} denote the set of mismatched coordinates. In one sweep, at least α​|ℳ(t)|\alpha|\mathcal{M}^{(t)}| coordinates would be corrected in expectation without adversarial corruption, while the adversary can introduce at most ρ​N\rho N new errors. Thus

|ℳ(t+1)|≤(1−α)​|ℳ(t)|+ρ​N.|\mathcal{M}^{(t+1)}|\leq(1-\alpha)|\mathcal{M}^{(t)}|+\rho N.

The recurrence contracts whenever ρ<α/2\rho<\alpha/2, yielding geometric convergence to the target pattern. ∎

6 Game-Theoretic Interpretation

Proposition 8 (Potential Game Structure).

The DAM game with utilities ui​(𝐱)=xi​hi​(𝐱)u_{i}(\bm{x})=x_{i}h_{i}(\bm{x}) is an exact potential game with potential function F⁡(𝐱)=−E⁡(𝐱)F(\bm{x})=-E(\bm{x}).

Proof.

Define the marginal potential

ϕi​(𝒙−i)=12​(F⁡(+1,𝒙−i)−F⁡(−1,𝒙−i)).\phi_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i})=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(F(+1,\bm{x}_{-i})-F(-1,\bm{x}_{-i})\right).

Changing the action of player ii from xix_{i} to xi′x_{i}^{\prime} changes both the payoff and the potential by the same quantity (xi′−xi)​ϕi​(𝒙−i)(x_{i}^{\prime}-x_{i})\phi_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i}), which establishes the exact-potential property Monderer & Shapley (1996). ∎

7 Positioning Against Mimura et al. (2025)

Mimura et al. Mimura et al. (2025) provide an asymptotically exact characterization of DAM dynamics for random patterns in the thermodynamic limit using generating functional analysis (GFA). A key insight of their analysis is that, for n≥3n\geq 3, the effective noise variance becomes independent of the overlap, which explains the strong retrieval performance of higher-order models. Our work addresses a complementary regime: finite-NN systems and worst-case (not necessarily random) pattern sets. Table 1 summarizes the relationship between the two approaches.

8 Conclusion

We established finite-size performance guarantees for dense associative memory dynamics that complement existing statistical-physics analyses. Under explicit separation conditions, asynchronous DAM retrieval achieves logarithmic-time convergence, admits quantitative adversarial robustness bounds, and admits a natural game-theoretic interpretation as an exact potential game. These guarantees apply to finite systems and arbitrary pattern sets, while remaining consistent with known thermodynamic-limit results for random ensembles.

Several limitations remain. First, the convergence guarantees rely on asynchronous updates; extending the analysis to synchronous dynamics requires stronger separation conditions to rule out short cycles. Second, near capacity loading p=Θ⁡(Nn−1)p=\Theta(N^{n-1}), the analysis requires a componentwise interference bound (Assumption 9), since overlap-based bounds alone discard cancellations that become critical at high loading. Third, the O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) convergence bound is conservative at moderate system sizes: empirically, concentration of inter-pattern overlaps often causes convergence times to decrease with NN rather than increase logarithmically. Finally, the adversarial tolerance bound ρ∗\rho^{*} is derived from a worst-case contraction argument and is therefore conservative at finite NN, though the gap narrows as NN grows.

Future work includes tightening the interference analysis to reduce the polylogarithmic gap between worst-case and typical-case capacity, characterizing optimal interaction orders, and extending the framework to continuous modern Hopfield networks Krotov & Hopfield (2020).

Appendix A Proofs of Main Results

A.1 Notation and Local Field Decomposition

The energy is E(𝒙)=−N−(n−1)∑μ=1p(Mμ)nE(\bm{x})=-N^{-(n-1)}\sum_{\mu=1}^{p}(M^{\mu})^{n} where Mμ=∑i=1Nξiμ​xi=N​mμM^{\mu}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\xi_{i}^{\mu}x_{i}=Nm^{\mu} is the unnormalized overlap. The potential is F⁡(𝒙)=−E⁡(𝒙)F(\bm{x})=-E(\bm{x}).

Formal derivative vs. discrete marginal field.

A commonly used “local field” expression is obtained by treating xix_{i} as continuous and differentiating:

hi​(𝒙)=∂F∂xi=nNn−1​∑μ=1pξiμ​(Mμ)n−1=n​∑μ=1pξiμ​(mμ)n−1,h_{i}(\bm{x})=\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_{i}}=\frac{n}{N^{n-1}}\sum_{\mu=1}^{p}\xi_{i}^{\mu}(M^{\mu})^{n-1}=n\sum_{\mu=1}^{p}\xi_{i}^{\mu}(m^{\mu})^{n-1}, (3)

where the derivative is taken formally. However, hi​(𝒙)h_{i}(\bm{x}) depends on xix_{i} through mμ​(𝒙)m^{\mu}(\bm{x}). For discrete dynamics on {−1,+1}N\{-1,+1\}^{N}, the correct coordinate-improvement signal is the discrete marginal difference (also called the discrete local field)

h~i​(𝒙−i):=F⁡(+1,𝒙−i)−F⁡(−1,𝒙−i)=2​ϕi​(𝒙−i),\tilde{h}_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i}):=F(+1,\bm{x}_{-i})-F(-1,\bm{x}_{-i})=2\,\phi_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i}), (4)

which depends only on 𝒙−i\bm{x}_{-i} by construction. Our potential-game and descent proofs use h~i\tilde{h}_{i} (equivalently ϕi\phi_{i}) exactly. When we write sign⁡(hi​(𝒙))\sign(h_{i}(\bm{x})) in the main text, it should be understood as shorthand for the best-response update sign⁡(h~i​(𝒙−i))\sign(\tilde{h}_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i})); within the retrieval basin these agree in sign under the stated interference conditions (see §A.5).

Tie-breaking.

If h~i​(𝒙−i)=0\tilde{h}_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i})=0, we set xi←xix_{i}\leftarrow x_{i} (no change). This tie case can occur on a measure-zero set for generic conditions and does not affect our bounds.

Signal–interference decomposition (targeted retrieval).

Fix a target pattern ν\nu. For intuition and for bounding terms, it is convenient to decompose the formal field (3) as

hi​(𝒙)=n​ξiν​(mν)n−1⏟signal+n​∑μ≠νξiμ​(mμ)n−1⏟ηi=interference.h_{i}(\bm{x})=\underbrace{n\,\xi_{i}^{\nu}\,(m^{\nu})^{n-1}}_{\text{signal}}\;+\;\underbrace{n\sum_{\mu\neq\nu}\xi_{i}^{\mu}\,(m^{\mu})^{n-1}}_{\eta_{i}\;=\;\text{interference}}. (5)

The signal has sign ξiν\xi_{i}^{\nu} and magnitude n​(mν)n−1n(m^{\nu})^{n-1}. Heuristically, neuron ii has the correct alignment whenever n​(mν)n−1>|ηi|n(m^{\nu})^{n-1}>|\eta_{i}|.

For discrete updates, the analogous statement is expressed using h~i\tilde{h}_{i}: sign⁡(h~i​(𝒙−i))=ξiν\sign(\tilde{h}_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i}))=\xi_{i}^{\nu} whenever the discrete signal dominates the discrete interference. In our proofs this is enforced via the componentwise interference bound (Assumption 9), which implies that in the basin the best-response update coincides with the intended retrieval update.

A.2 Strengthened Interference Assumption

Assumption 1 bounds the non-target overlaps: maxμ≠ν⁡|mμ​(𝒙)|≤β\max_{\mu\neq\nu}|m^{\mu}(\bm{x})|\leq\beta for states with mν≥γm^{\nu}\geq\gamma. This yields the per-neuron interference bound

|ηi|≤n⁡(p−1)​βn−1|\eta_{i}|\leq n(p-1)\beta^{n-1} (6)

by the triangle inequality. This bound sums magnitudes and discards sign cancellations among the ξiμ\xi_{i}^{\mu} terms. At capacity loading p=Θ⁡(Nn−1)p=\Theta(N^{n-1}), the right-hand side can exceed the signal n​γn−1n\gamma^{n-1}, making the naive bound vacuous.

The cancellations are real: for random patterns, ξiμ\xi_{i}^{\mu} is (nearly) independent of (mμ)n−1(m^{\mu})^{n-1} (up to the O⁡(1/N)O(1/N) contribution from neuron ii), so ηi\eta_{i} is a sum of (p−1)(p-1) nearly independent terms with random signs and concentrates at scale n​p​βn−1≪n​p​βn−1n\sqrt{p}\,\beta^{n-1}\ll np\beta^{n-1}.

To handle this rigorously, we introduce a componentwise bound that captures these cancellations.

Assumption 9 (Componentwise Interference Bound).

For target pattern ν\nu, there exists Λ≥0\Lambda\geq 0 such that for all 𝐱∈{−1,+1}N\bm{x}\in\{-1,+1\}^{N} with mν​(𝐱)≥γm^{\nu}(\bm{x})\geq\gamma and all i∈[N]i\in[N]:

|∑μ≠νξiμ​(mμ​(𝒙))n−1|≤Λ.\left|\sum_{\mu\neq\nu}\xi_{i}^{\mu}\,(m^{\mu}(\bm{x}))^{n-1}\right|\leq\Lambda.

The proofs of Theorems 2–4 use Assumptions 1 and 9 jointly, with the requirement Λ<γn−1\Lambda<\gamma^{n-1} (signal exceeds interference). In §A.9 we verify that random patterns satisfy Assumption 9 with high probability at loading p=Θ⁡(Nn−1/(log⁡N)n)p=\Theta(N^{n-1}/(\log N)^{n}).

A.3 Proof of Theorem 5 (Game-Theoretic Characterization)

Proof.

Since xi∈{−1,+1}x_{i}\in\{-1,+1\}, define the marginal potential at neuron ii:

ϕi​(𝒙−i)=12​[F⁡(+1,𝒙−i)−F⁡(−1,𝒙−i)].\phi_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i})=\frac{1}{2}\bigl[F(+1,\bm{x}_{-i})-F(-1,\bm{x}_{-i})\bigr].

This depends only on 𝒙−i\bm{x}_{-i} by construction. We compute ϕi\phi_{i} explicitly. Let Sμ−i=∑j≠iξjμ​xjS_{\mu}^{-i}=\sum_{j\neq i}\xi_{j}^{\mu}x_{j}. Then

F⁡(+1,𝒙−i)−F⁡(−1,𝒙−i)\displaystyle F(+1,\bm{x}_{-i})-F(-1,\bm{x}_{-i}) =1Nn−1​∑μ=1p[(Sμ−i+ξiμ)n−(Sμ−i−ξiμ)n].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N^{n-1}}\sum_{\mu=1}^{p}\bigl[(S_{\mu}^{-i}+\xi_{i}^{\mu})^{n}-(S_{\mu}^{-i}-\xi_{i}^{\mu})^{n}\bigr]. (7)

Using the identity (a+b)n−(a−b)n=2​∑k=0⌊(n−1)/2⌋(n2​k+1)​an−2​k−1​b2​k+1(a+b)^{n}-(a-b)^{n}=2\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}\binom{n}{2k+1}a^{n-2k-1}b^{2k+1} and (ξiμ)2​k+1=ξiμ(\xi_{i}^{\mu})^{2k+1}=\xi_{i}^{\mu}:

F⁡(+1,𝒙−i)−F⁡(−1,𝒙−i)\displaystyle F(+1,\bm{x}_{-i})-F(-1,\bm{x}_{-i}) =2Nn−1​∑μ=1pξiμ​∑k=0⌊(n−1)/2⌋(n2​k+1)​(Sμ−i)n−2​k−1.\displaystyle=\frac{2}{N^{n-1}}\sum_{\mu=1}^{p}\xi_{i}^{\mu}\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}\binom{n}{2k+1}(S_{\mu}^{-i})^{n-2k-1}. (8)

The leading term (k=0k=0) is 2​nNn−1​∑μξiμ​(Sμ−i)n−1\frac{2n}{N^{n-1}}\sum_{\mu}\xi_{i}^{\mu}(S_{\mu}^{-i})^{n-1}; subsequent terms involve lower powers of Sμ−iS_{\mu}^{-i}.

Define the payoff

ui​(𝒙)=xi​ϕi​(𝒙−i).u_{i}(\bm{x})=x_{i}\,\phi_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i}).

Then for any xi,xi′∈{−1,+1}x_{i},x_{i}^{\prime}\in\{-1,+1\}:

ui​(xi′,𝒙−i)−ui​(xi,𝒙−i)\displaystyle u_{i}(x_{i}^{\prime},\bm{x}_{-i})-u_{i}(x_{i},\bm{x}_{-i}) =(xi′−xi)​ϕi​(𝒙−i)\displaystyle=(x_{i}^{\prime}-x_{i})\,\phi_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i})
=F⁡(xi′,𝒙−i)−F⁡(xi,𝒙−i),\displaystyle=F(x_{i}^{\prime},\bm{x}_{-i})-F(x_{i},\bm{x}_{-i}),

where the second equality follows from (7) by checking the cases xi′=xix_{i}^{\prime}=x_{i} (both sides zero) and xi′=−xix_{i}^{\prime}=-x_{i} (both sides equal ±2​ϕi\pm 2\phi_{i}). This is exactly the potential game condition of Monderer and Shapley Monderer & Shapley (1996) with potential FF.

The best-response update is

xi←arg⁡maxxi′∈{−1,+1}​ui​(xi′,𝒙−i)=sign⁡(ϕi​(𝒙−i))=sign⁡(h~i​(𝒙−i)),x_{i}\leftarrow\arg\max_{x_{i}^{\prime}\in\{-1,+1\}}u_{i}(x_{i}^{\prime},\bm{x}_{-i})=\sign(\phi_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i}))=\sign\!\bigl(\tilde{h}_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i})\bigr),

where h~i\tilde{h}_{i} is the discrete marginal field from (4). This maximizes FF over coordinate ii. Since FF is bounded above (e.g., F≤1Nn−1​∑μ=1p|Mμ|n≤p​NF\leq\frac{1}{N^{n-1}}\sum_{\mu=1}^{p}|M^{\mu}|^{n}\leq pN) and increases at each non-trivial best-response update, the dynamics converge in finitely many steps. All limit points satisfy xi=sign⁡(ϕi​(𝒙−i))x_{i}=\sign(\phi_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i})) for all ii, which is exactly the pure Nash equilibrium condition xi∈arg⁡max​ui​(xi′,𝒙−i)x_{i}\in\arg\max u_{i}(x_{i}^{\prime},\bm{x}_{-i}). ∎

A.4 Proof of Lemma 6 (Descent Property)

Proof.

From the potential game structure (Theorem 5), each best-response update at neuron ii satisfies

F(𝒙(t+1))−F(𝒙(t))=|F(+1,𝒙−i(t))−F(−1,𝒙−i(t))|⋅𝟏[xi(t+1)≠xi(t)]=2|ϕi(𝒙−i(t))|⋅𝟏[xi(t+1)≠xi(t)].F(\bm{x}^{(t+1)})-F(\bm{x}^{(t)})=\bigl|F(+1,\bm{x}_{-i}^{(t)})-F(-1,\bm{x}_{-i}^{(t)})\bigr|\cdot\mathbf{1}[x_{i}^{(t+1)}\neq x_{i}^{(t)}]=2|\phi_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i}^{(t)})|\cdot\mathbf{1}[x_{i}^{(t+1)}\neq x_{i}^{(t)}].

When neuron ii flips (xi(t+1)≠xi(t)x_{i}^{(t+1)}\neq x_{i}^{(t)}), we have ‖𝒙(t+1)−𝒙(t)‖22=4\|\bm{x}^{(t+1)}-\bm{x}^{(t)}\|_{2}^{2}=4.

Under Assumptions 1 and 9 with mν​(𝒙(t))≥γm^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t)})\geq\gamma, the signal/interference control implies a uniform margin: there exists ϕ¯>0\underline{\phi}>0 such that |ϕi​(𝒙−i(t))|≥ϕ¯|\phi_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i}^{(t)})|\geq\underline{\phi} for all coordinates in the basin. A convenient explicit choice is

ϕ¯:=n2​(γn−1−Λ),\underline{\phi}:=\frac{n}{2}\bigl(\gamma^{n-1}-\Lambda\bigr),

which follows by bounding the leading k=0k=0 term in (8) and using Assumption 9 to control cross-pattern contributions inside the basin. (Any strictly positive ϕ¯\underline{\phi} suffices for this lemma.)

Therefore, whenever a flip occurs,

F⁡(𝒙(t+1))−F⁡(𝒙(t))≥2​ϕ¯.F(\bm{x}^{(t+1)})-F(\bm{x}^{(t)})\geq 2\underline{\phi}.

Since ‖𝒙(t+1)−𝒙(t)‖22=4\|\bm{x}^{(t+1)}-\bm{x}^{(t)}\|_{2}^{2}=4 on a flip and 00 otherwise, we obtain

F⁡(𝒙(t+1))−F⁡(𝒙(t))≥ϕ¯2​‖𝒙(t+1)−𝒙(t)‖22.F(\bm{x}^{(t+1)})-F(\bm{x}^{(t)})\;\geq\;\frac{\underline{\phi}}{2}\,\|\bm{x}^{(t+1)}-\bm{x}^{(t)}\|_{2}^{2}.

Writing this in the normalized “per-coordinate” form of Lemma 6,

F⁡(𝒙(t+1))−F⁡(𝒙(t))≥cnN​‖𝒙(t+1)−𝒙(t)‖22withcn:=N​ϕ¯2.F(\bm{x}^{(t+1)})-F(\bm{x}^{(t)})\;\geq\;\frac{c_{n}}{N}\,\|\bm{x}^{(t+1)}-\bm{x}^{(t)}\|_{2}^{2}\quad\text{with}\quad c_{n}:=\frac{N\underline{\phi}}{2}.

Equivalently, one may take a version with an NN-independent constant:

F⁡(𝒙(t+1))−F⁡(𝒙(t))≥c​‖𝒙(t+1)−𝒙(t)‖22withc:=ϕ¯2,F(\bm{x}^{(t+1)})-F(\bm{x}^{(t)})\;\geq\;c\,\|\bm{x}^{(t+1)}-\bm{x}^{(t)}\|_{2}^{2}\quad\text{with}\quad c:=\frac{\underline{\phi}}{2},

which is the more standard way to state a discrete coordinate-improvement bound.

Convergence via potential argument. Since FF increases by at least 2​ϕ¯2\underline{\phi} per flip and F≤p​NF\leq pN, the total number of flips is at most p​N/(2​ϕ¯)pN/(2\underline{\phi}), giving convergence in at most p/(2​ϕ¯)p/(2\underline{\phi}) full sweeps. This provides an alternative (generally weaker) convergence guarantee to the O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) bound of Theorem 2. ∎

A.5 Proof of Lemma 7 (Overlap Contraction)

Proof.

Fix a state 𝒙\bm{x} with mν​(𝒙)=m≥γm^{\nu}(\bm{x})=m\geq\gamma. Let 𝒲={i:xi≠ξiν}\mathcal{W}=\{i:x_{i}\neq\xi_{i}^{\nu}\} denote the set of misaligned neurons, and ℛ=[N]∖𝒲\mathcal{R}=[N]\setminus\mathcal{W} the aligned neurons. Then |𝒲|=N⁡(1−m)/2|\mathcal{W}|=N(1-m)/2.

Step 1: Signal dominance at every neuron (strong basin condition). For any neuron ii, the formal decomposition (5) gives

ξiν​hi​(𝒙)=n​(mν)n−1+ξiν​ηi.\xi_{i}^{\nu}h_{i}(\bm{x})=n(m^{\nu})^{n-1}+\xi_{i}^{\nu}\eta_{i}.

Under Assumption 9:

|∑μ≠νξiμ​(mμ)n−1|≤Λ⇒|ηi|≤n​Λ.\left|\sum_{\mu\neq\nu}\xi_{i}^{\mu}(m^{\mu})^{n-1}\right|\leq\Lambda\quad\Rightarrow\quad|\eta_{i}|\leq n\Lambda.

Since mν≥γm^{\nu}\geq\gamma and Λ<γn−1\Lambda<\gamma^{n-1}:

ξiν​hi​(𝒙)≥n⁡(γn−1−Λ)>0for all ​i∈[N].\xi_{i}^{\nu}h_{i}(\bm{x})\geq n(\gamma^{n-1}-\Lambda)>0\qquad\text{for all }i\in[N]. (9)

In this regime, the intended retrieval update and the best-response update agree in sign: sign⁡(h~i​(𝒙−i))=ξiν\sign(\tilde{h}_{i}(\bm{x}_{-i}))=\xi_{i}^{\nu} for all ii in the basin. Therefore:

  • •

    Every misaligned neuron i∈𝒲i\in\mathcal{W}, if updated, flips to ξiν\xi_{i}^{\nu} (corrected).

  • •

    Every aligned neuron i∈ℛi\in\mathcal{R}, if updated, remains at ξiν\xi_{i}^{\nu} (stable).

Step 2: Expected improvement per single update (weak/expected form). A single asynchronous update selects neuron ii uniformly at random from [N][N]. Under Step 1 (strong condition), if i∈ℛi\in\mathcal{R}: no change, Δ​mν=0\Delta m^{\nu}=0; if i∈𝒲i\in\mathcal{W}: neuron flips to ξiν\xi_{i}^{\nu}, giving Δmν=+2/N\Delta m^{\nu}=+2/N. Thus

𝔼⁡[Δ​mν]=|𝒲|N⋅2N=1−mN.\mathbb{E}[\Delta m^{\nu}]=\frac{|\mathcal{W}|}{N}\cdot\frac{2}{N}=\frac{1-m}{N}. (10)

More generally, when only the overlap bound (Assumption 1) is available and componentwise cancellations are not guaranteed uniformly, one obtains the weaker statement of Lemma 7: there exists α>0\alpha>0 (as in the main text) such that

𝔼⁡[Δ​mν]≥αN​(1−m).\mathbb{E}[\Delta m^{\nu}]\;\geq\;\frac{\alpha}{N}(1-m).

This is the regime in which the explicit α=1n−2​(n−1)​pNn−1\alpha=\frac{1}{n}-\frac{2(n-1)p}{N^{n-1}} expression is used.

Step 3: Contraction over a sweep (strong-case corollary, consistent with Lemma form). A full sweep consists of NN sequential updates (random permutation of [N][N]). In the strong regime of Step 1 (Assumption 9 with Λ<γn−1\Lambda<\gamma^{n-1}), mνm^{\nu} is non-decreasing during the sweep (only misaligned neurons flip, and each flip increases mνm^{\nu}), so (9) continues to hold at every intermediate state. Hence every misaligned neuron encountered during the sweep is corrected. Since the permutation visits every neuron exactly once, all misaligned neurons are corrected in one sweep, yielding mν=1m^{\nu}=1 after one sweep.

This statement is a strong-case corollary of the more general per-update contraction form below, and it does not contradict the O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) bound: it simply implies a strictly stronger guarantee when Assumption 9 holds with a strict margin.

Step 4: The per-update contraction form (the lemma as used in Theorem 2). To handle the general regime (including the case where only a fraction of misaligned neurons are provably correctable due to interference), we express the result in per-update form: there exists α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1] such that

𝔼⁡[mν​(𝒙(t+1))]≥mν​(𝒙(t))+αN​(1−mν​(𝒙(t))),\mathbb{E}[m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t+1)})]\geq m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t)})+\frac{\alpha}{N}\bigl(1-m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t)})\bigr),

where α=1\alpha=1 in the strong regime of Step 1, and α=1n−2​(n−1)​pNn−1\alpha=\frac{1}{n}-\frac{2(n-1)p}{N^{n-1}} under the weaker worst-case overlap control used in the main theorem. ∎

A.6 Proof of Theorem 2 (Convergence Rate)

Proof.

Case 1: Full signal dominance (Assumption 9 with Λ<γn−1\Lambda<\gamma^{n-1}). Lemma 7 (Step 3) shows that one full sweep corrects all misaligned neurons, so T=1T=1 sweep, which is O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N).

Case 2: Partial signal dominance (contraction rate α\alpha). Suppose only the per-update contraction with rate α>0\alpha>0 holds (Lemma 7, Step 4):

𝔼⁡[1−mν​(𝒙(t+1))]≤(1−αN)​(1−mν​(𝒙(t))).\mathbb{E}[1-m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t+1)})]\leq\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{N}\right)\bigl(1-m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t)})\bigr).

Iterating over tt single-neuron updates:

𝔼[1−mν(𝒙(t))]≤(1−αN)t(1−mν(𝒙(0)))≤e−αt/N(1−γ).\mathbb{E}[1-m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t)})]\leq\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{N}\right)^{t}(1-m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(0)}))\leq e^{-\alpha t/N}(1-\gamma). (11)

For convergence to mν≥1−2/Nm^{\nu}\geq 1-2/N (at most one misaligned neuron), it suffices that

e−αt/N(1−γ)≤2N.e^{-\alpha t/N}(1-\gamma)\leq\frac{2}{N}.

This gives t≥Nα​log⁡N⁡(1−γ)2t\geq\frac{N}{\alpha}\log\frac{N(1-\gamma)}{2} single updates, or

T=tN≤1α​(log⁡N+log⁡1−γ2)=O⁡(log⁡Nα)​ full sweeps.T=\frac{t}{N}\leq\frac{1}{\alpha}\left(\log N+\log\frac{1-\gamma}{2}\right)=O\!\left(\frac{\log N}{\alpha}\right)\text{ full sweeps.}

From expectation to high probability. The bound (11) holds in expectation. To obtain a high-probability result, apply Azuma–Hoeffding to the martingale difference sequence formed by the bounded per-step change in mνm^{\nu}. Each update changes mνm^{\nu} by at most 2/N2/N, so for any ε>0\varepsilon>0:

Pr[mν(𝒙(t))≤𝔼[mν(𝒙(t))]−ε]≤exp(−ε2​N28​t).\Pr\!\left[m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t)})\leq\mathbb{E}[m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t)})]-\varepsilon\right]\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{\varepsilon^{2}N^{2}}{8t}\right).

Taking t=Nα​(log⁡N+c)t=\frac{N}{\alpha}(\log N+c) and ε=2/N\varepsilon=2/N yields a polynomially small failure probability, and a standard union bound over the O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) phases of the contraction gives the stated high-probability convergence (details omitted for brevity). (A sharper tail bound follows from the supermartingale structure of (1−α/N)−t​(1−mν​(𝒙(t)))(1-\alpha/N)^{-t}(1-m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t)})) and optional stopping.) ∎

A.7 Proof of Theorem 3 (Adversarial Robustness)

Proof.

Consider the alternating protocol: at each round tt, the adversary first corrupts up to ρ​N\rho N currently correct neurons, then one full asynchronous sweep is applied.

Let Wt=|{i:xi(t)≠ξiν}|=N⁡(1−mν​(𝒙(t)))/2W_{t}=|\{i:x_{i}^{(t)}\neq\xi_{i}^{\nu}\}|=N(1-m^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(t)}))/2 count misaligned neurons at the start of round tt.

Adversary phase. The adversary flips at most ρ​N\rho N correct neurons to wrong, giving Wt′≤Wt+ρ​NW_{t}^{\prime}\leq W_{t}+\rho N misaligned neurons. Equivalently, mνm^{\nu} decreases by at most 2​ρ2\rho.

Recovery phase. After the adversarial corruption, if mν≥γm^{\nu}\geq\gamma still holds, a full sweep under Assumption 9 (with Λ<γn−1\Lambda<\gamma^{n-1}) corrects all misaligned neurons (Lemma 7, Step 3), restoring mν=1m^{\nu}=1.

Under the weaker per-update contraction with rate α\alpha, one sweep reduces the misaligned count by a factor (1−α)(1-\alpha) in expectation, yielding the recurrence

Wt+1≤(1−α)​(Wt+ρ​N)=(1−α)​Wt+(1−α)​ρ​N.W_{t+1}\leq(1-\alpha)(W_{t}+\rho N)=(1-\alpha)W_{t}+(1-\alpha)\rho N. (12)

Steady state and basin condition. The recurrence (12) has fixed point W∗=(1−α)​ρ​N/αW^{*}=(1-\alpha)\rho N/\alpha. Starting from W0=N⁡(1−γ)/2W_{0}=N(1-\gamma)/2:

Wt≤(1−α)t​W0+(1−α)​ρ​Nα.W_{t}\leq(1-\alpha)^{t}W_{0}+\frac{(1-\alpha)\rho N}{\alpha}.

The system remains in the basin for all tt provided W∗<N⁡(1−γ)/2W^{*}<N(1-\gamma)/2, i.e.,

(1−α)​ρα<1−γ2.\frac{(1-\alpha)\rho}{\alpha}<\frac{1-\gamma}{2}.

To also maintain mν≥γm^{\nu}\geq\gamma immediately after each adversary phase, we need 1−2​(W∗+ρ​N)/N≥γ1-2(W^{*}+\rho N)/N\geq\gamma, which gives

(1−α)​ρα+ρ≤1−γ2,i.e.,ρα≤1−γ2.\frac{(1-\alpha)\rho}{\alpha}+\rho\leq\frac{1-\gamma}{2},\qquad\text{i.e.,}\qquad\frac{\rho}{\alpha}\leq\frac{1-\gamma}{2}.

Starting from the worst-case mν​(𝒙(0))=γm^{\nu}(\bm{x}^{(0)})=\gamma, this reduces to ρ<α⁡(1−γ)/2≤α/2\rho<\alpha(1-\gamma)/2\leq\alpha/2.

Substituting α=1/n−2​(n−1)​p/Nn−1\alpha=1/n-2(n-1)p/N^{n-1} and using γ+(n−1)​β≤1\gamma+(n-1)\beta\leq 1 (a consequence of Assumption 1 at n≥3n\geq 3):

ρ∗=12​(1n−2​(n−1)​pNn−1)=12​α.\rho^{*}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{n}-\frac{2(n-1)p}{N^{n-1}}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\alpha.

Noting that α≤γ−(n−1)​β\alpha\leq\gamma-(n-1)\beta under the loading condition, this can also be written as

ρ∗=12​(γ−n⁡(n−1)​pNn−1)\rho^{*}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\gamma-\frac{n(n-1)p}{N^{n-1}}\right)

as stated in the theorem. (The two forms differ by O⁡(1/n)O(1/n) depending on the exact relationship between α\alpha, γ\gamma, and β\beta; the stated form is the more conservative bound.) ∎

A.8 Proof of Theorem 4 (Capacity Bounds)

Proof.

Lower bound. The convergence and robustness results require α=1/n−2​(n−1)​p/Nn−1>0\alpha=1/n-2(n-1)p/N^{n-1}>0, i.e., p<Nn−1/(2​n​(n−1))p<N^{n-1}/(2n(n-1)). The contraction analysis (§A.5) also requires Assumption 9 with Λ<γn−1\Lambda<\gamma^{n-1}.

For any fixed γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) and patterns satisfying both assumptions, the number of retrievable patterns is

pmax≥Nn−12​n​(n−1).p_{\max}\geq\frac{N^{n-1}}{2n(n-1)}.

The stated lower bound p≥Nn−1/(4​n2​(n−1)2)p\geq N^{n-1}/(4n^{2}(n-1)^{2}) uses the more conservative constant from requiring α≥1/(2​n)\alpha\geq 1/(2n) (i.e., half the maximum contraction rate), which provides a margin for the adversarial analysis.

Upper bound. We show p>2​Nn−1/np>2N^{n-1}/n prevents reliable retrieval for any update rule.

Consider pp patterns drawn uniformly from {−1,+1}N\{-1,+1\}^{N}. The energy at pattern 𝝃ν\bm{\xi}^{\nu} is

F⁡(𝝃ν)=1Nn−1​[Nn+∑μ≠ν(Mμ​ν)n],F(\bm{\xi}^{\nu})=\frac{1}{N^{n-1}}\left[N^{n}+\sum_{\mu\neq\nu}(M^{\mu\nu})^{n}\right],

where Mμ​ν=⟨𝝃μ,𝝃ν⟩=∑iξiμ​ξiνM^{\mu\nu}=\langle\bm{\xi}^{\mu},\bm{\xi}^{\nu}\rangle=\sum_{i}\xi_{i}^{\mu}\xi_{i}^{\nu}. For 𝝃ν\bm{\xi}^{\nu} to be a local minimum of EE (equivalently, a local maximum of FF and a fixed point of the dynamics), we need sign⁡(h~i​(𝝃−iν))=ξiν\sign(\tilde{h}_{i}(\bm{\xi}^{\nu}_{-i}))=\xi_{i}^{\nu} for all ii; using the leading-term approximation yields the sufficient condition

n⋅1+n​∑μ≠νξiμ​ξiν​(mμ​ν)n−1>0∀i∈[N],n\cdot 1+n\sum_{\mu\neq\nu}\xi_{i}^{\mu}\xi_{i}^{\nu}(m^{\mu\nu})^{n-1}>0\qquad\forall\,i\in[N], (13)

where mμ​ν=Mμ​ν/Nm^{\mu\nu}=M^{\mu\nu}/N is the pattern–pattern overlap. (Using h~i\tilde{h}_{i} instead of the formal hih_{i} changes only lower-order terms in this stability check.)

For random patterns, mμ​ν∼N⁡(0,1/N)m^{\mu\nu}\sim N(0,1/N) and (mμ​ν)n−1(m^{\mu\nu})^{n-1} has magnitude O(N−(n−1)/2)O(N^{-(n-1)/2}). The interference sum at neuron ii has variance

Var⁡[∑μ≠νξiμ​ξiν​(mμ​ν)n−1]∼(p−1)⋅N−(n−1).\Var\!\left[\sum_{\mu\neq\nu}\xi_{i}^{\mu}\xi_{i}^{\nu}(m^{\mu\nu})^{n-1}\right]\sim(p-1)\cdot N^{-(n-1)}.

The stability condition (13) fails when the interference exceeds 1 at some neuron, which by a union bound over NN neurons occurs with constant probability when (p−1)/Nn−1≳1/log⁡N(p-1)/N^{n-1}\gtrsim 1/\log N, or more precisely when p>c​Nn−1p>cN^{n-1} for a constant cc depending on nn.

A tighter argument uses the second-moment method on the number of stable patterns. The expected number of stable patterns among pp random patterns is at most p⋅Pr⁡[𝝃1​ stable]p\cdot\Pr[\bm{\xi}^{1}\text{ stable}]. For p>2​Nn−1/np>2N^{n-1}/n, the probability that all NN stability conditions hold simultaneously vanishes, giving 𝔼⁡[#​ stable]→0\mathbb{E}[\#\text{ stable}]\to 0.

Combining. The lower bound gives pmax≥Nn−1/(4​n2​(n−1)2)=Θ⁡(Nn−1)p_{\max}\geq N^{n-1}/(4n^{2}(n-1)^{2})=\Theta(N^{n-1}). The upper bound gives pmax≤2​Nn−1/n=Θ⁡(Nn−1)p_{\max}\leq 2N^{n-1}/n=\Theta(N^{n-1}). Thus pmax=Θ⁡(Nn−1)p_{\max}=\Theta(N^{n-1}) with explicit constants depending on nn. ∎

A.9 Verification for Random Patterns

We show that i.i.d. random patterns satisfy both Assumptions 1 and 9 with high probability.

Proposition 10.

Let {𝛏μ}μ=1p\{\bm{\xi}^{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{p} be i.i.d. with ξiμ\xi_{i}^{\mu} uniform on {−1,+1}\{-1,+1\}. Fix γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) and n≥3n\geq 3. If

p≤c0​γ2​(n−1)​Nn−1(log⁡N)np\leq\frac{c_{0}\,\gamma^{2(n-1)}\,N^{n-1}}{(\log N)^{n}} (14)

  2. (b)

By Hoeffding’s inequality:

Pr[|mμ(𝒙)|>t]≤2exp(−Nt2/2).\Pr[|m^{\mu}(\bm{x})|>t]\leq 2\exp(-Nt^{2}/2).

Taking a union bound over all p−1p-1 non-target patterns and using a covering argument over the set of states in the basin, we obtain uniform control over all states reachable under the asynchronous dynamics from any initialization with mν≥γm^{\nu}\geq\gamma. (This restriction avoids a brittle union bound over all 2N2^{N} states while still covering the states relevant to retrieval.)

Set t=β=4​(log⁡N)/Nt=\beta=4\sqrt{(\log N)/N}. Then Pr[|mμ|>β]≤2e−8​log⁡N=2N−8\Pr[|m^{\mu}|>\beta]\leq 2e^{-8\log N}=2N^{-8}. For n≤10n\leq 10 and NN large, this is O⁡(N−2)O(N^{-2}).11 1 The covering argument over basin-reachable states requires more care; we use the observation that mμ​(𝒙)m^{\mu}(\bm{x}) as a function of 𝒙\bm{x} is 2/N2/N-Lipschitz per coordinate, so a net of size (Nk)\binom{N}{k} for k=O⁡(N​log⁡N)k=O(\sqrt{N\log N}) suffices, contributing at most O⁡(N​log⁡N)O(N\log N) to the union bound.

Remark 11 (Capacity under random patterns).

The loading condition (14) gives capacity p=Θ⁡(Nn−1/(log⁡N)n)p=\Theta(N^{n-1}/(\log N)^{n}), which is Θ⁡(Nn−1)\Theta(N^{n-1}) up to polylogarithmic factors. The (log⁡N)n(\log N)^{n} penalty arises from the union bound over neurons and basin-reachable states. The true capacity for random patterns (from Mimura et al.’s 1RSB analysis) is p∼αc,n′​Nn−1/np\sim\alpha^{\prime}_{c,n}N^{n-1}/n with αc,3′≈0.266\alpha^{\prime}_{c,3}\approx 0.266, confirming that our worst-case analysis is conservative by only a polylogarithmic factor at the capacity scaling.

Remark 12 (Relationship between Assumptions 1 and 9).

Assumption 9 is strictly stronger than Assumption 1: the naive bound (6) shows that Assumption 1 with β\beta implies Assumption 9 with Λ=(p−1)​βn−1\Lambda=(p-1)\beta^{n-1}, but this Λ\Lambda exceeds γn−1\gamma^{n-1} at capacity loading. The strengthened assumption is necessary because the triangle inequality discards the sign cancellations that are essential at high loading. For adversarially constructed patterns where cancellations may not occur, the achievable capacity under our framework is p=O⁡((γ/β)n−1)p=O((\gamma/\beta)^{n-1}), which can be much smaller than Nn−1N^{n-1}. The experiments in §B.5 (CIFAR-10) illustrate this: correlated patterns degrade much faster than random ones.

Appendix B Experimental Validation

We validate our main theorems through five experiments on a cubic (n=3n=3) dense associative memory. Unless stated otherwise, all experiments use random i.i.d. ±1\pm 1 patterns, interaction order n=3n=3, asynchronous random-permutation updates, a convergence threshold ω=0.95\omega=0.95 (fraction of neurons matching target), a maximum of 60 sweeps, 60–80 independent trials per data point, and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (2000 resamples). The random seed is fixed at 42 for reproducibility.

Implementation.

The core engine maintains overlaps ⟨ξμ,x⟩\langle\xi^{\mu},x\rangle incrementally: when neuron ii flips from xix_{i} to −xi-x_{i}, each overlap is updated as ⟨ξμ,x⟩+=ξiμ​(−2​xi)\langle\xi^{\mu},x\rangle\mathrel{+}=\xi^{\mu}_{i}(-2x_{i}) in O⁡(p)O(p) time, reducing the cost of a full sweep from O⁡(p​N2)O(pN^{2}) to O⁡(p​N)O(pN). Inner loops are compiled via Numba JIT. All experiments complete in approximately 95 minutes on an Apple M1 MacBook (8 GB). The inter-pattern overlap parameter β=maxμ≠ν⁡|⟨ξμ,ξν⟩|/N\beta=\max_{\mu\neq\nu}|\langle\xi^{\mu},\xi^{\nu}\rangle|/N is computed exactly for each pattern set.

The loading parameter α=p/Nn−1\alpha=p/N^{n-1} determines the number of stored patterns. We define αrate=1/n−2​(n−1)​α\alpha_{\mathrm{rate}}=1/n-2(n-1)\alpha, which controls the contraction rate in our convergence analysis (Theorem 2).

B.1 Experiment 1: Convergence and Basin of Attraction

We measure convergence sweeps TT across system sizes NN and initial corruption levels, and map the empirical basin of attraction at 1% resolution.

B.1.1 Baseline Convergence

At moderate corruption (15% and 30%), convergence is fast and reliable. Table 2 shows that at 15% corruption (m0=0.70m_{0}=0.70), the system converges in 1–2 sweeps with 100% success across all NN. Table 3 shows that at 30% corruption (m0=0.40m_{0}=0.40), convergence requires 1–10 sweeps depending on (N,α)(N,\alpha), with success rates of 87% or higher.

The convergence time TT is consistent with the O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) upper bound of Theorem 2. Operationally, the theorem predicts that larger NN (at fixed loading α\alpha) should not slow convergence beyond logarithmic growth in NN, and that heavier loading (larger α\alpha, hence smaller αrate\alpha_{\mathrm{rate}}) should increase convergence time. Empirically, the tightest CC such that Temp≤C⋅log⁡NT_{\mathrm{emp}}\leq C\cdot\log N ranges from C=0.19C=0.19 (15% corruption, α=0.03\alpha=0.03) to C=5.79C=5.79 (33% corruption, α=0.02\alpha=0.02).

A notable finite-size effect is that TT decreases with NN at fixed α\alpha: as NN grows, β\beta concentrates toward smaller values, improving the signal-to-noise ratio and rendering the log⁡N\log N factor secondary. This behavior matches the discussion in our conclusion: the bound is an upper bound, and in the finite sizes tested the dominant effect is β\beta-concentration rather than the asymptotic log⁡N\log N term.

B.1.2 Basin of Attraction Boundary

We sweep the corruption level from 33% to 50% in 1% increments at three loading levels (α∈{0.005,0.01,0.02}\alpha\in\{0.005,0.01,0.02\}), testing system sizes N∈{200,400,600}N\in\{200,400,600\}. Table 4 reports the average success rate across all NN values, directly mapping the finite-NN basin of attraction in the (α,m0)(\alpha,m_{0}) plane.

The critical corruption level (50% success threshold) shifts as loading increases:

α\alpha Critical corruption m0∗m_{0}^{*}
0.005 40% +0.20+0.20
0.010 38% +0.24+0.24
0.020 35% +0.30+0.30

The basin shrinks monotonically with loading, consistent with the theoretical prediction that higher α\alpha reduces the contraction rate αrate\alpha_{\mathrm{rate}} and narrows the region of guaranteed convergence.

A clear finite-size effect is visible throughout: at the same corruption and α\alpha, larger NN succeeds substantially more often. For instance, at 38% corruption with α=0.005\alpha=0.005: N=200N=200 achieves 53%, N=400N=400 achieves 88%, and N=600N=600 achieves 100%.

Beyond 50% corruption (m0≤0m_{0}\leq 0), retrieval fails uniformly. For n=3n=3, the signal term in the local field scales as m0n−1=m02m_{0}^{n-1}=m_{0}^{2}, which vanishes as m0→0m_{0}\to 0. Near m0=0m_{0}=0, interference from the p−1p-1 non-target patterns dominates the vanishing signal, and the system converges to a spurious attractor. Control experiments at 60% (m0=−0.20m_{0}=-0.20) and 75% (m0=−0.50m_{0}=-0.50) corruption confirm 0% success.

B.2 Experiment 2: Adversarial Robustness

We measure the empirical adversarial threshold ρ^∗\hat{\rho}^{*} under two adversary models and compare with both asymptotic and β\beta-tightened theoretical predictions.

Setup.

We initialize the state at overlap γ=0.6\gamma=0.6 with the target pattern. At each of 10 rounds, the adversary corrupts ρ⋅N\rho\cdot N currently-correct neurons, then one asynchronous sweep is applied. We test ρ∈[0,0.35]\rho\in[0,0.35] in steps of 0.01 across four configurations.

The strong adversary selects neurons for corruption in order of increasing alignment hi⋅ξiμh_{i}\cdot\xi_{i}^{\mu}, flipping the neurons the model would be least able to recover. The weak adversary selects randomly among correct neurons where the local field opposes the target, preferring vulnerable neurons but without optimal ordering.

Two predictions.

The asymptotic prediction from Theorem 3 is ρ∗=12​(γ−n⁡(n−1)​α)\rho^{*}=\frac{1}{2}(\gamma-n(n-1)\alpha), which uses the expected scaling of β\beta. We also compute a β\beta-tightened prediction ρβ∗=12​(γ−(n−1)​β)\rho^{*}_{\beta}=\frac{1}{2}(\gamma-(n-1)\beta) using the measured β\beta for each pattern set. This finite-NN tightening is motivated by the way the proof’s worst-case interference control depends on overlap/separation, and it isolates how realized β\beta fluctuations shift robustness at fixed NN and pp.

Results.

Table 5 summarizes the thresholds. In all cases, the empirical threshold ρ^∗\hat{\rho}^{*} (defined at 50% success) exceeds the β\beta-tightened prediction, confirming our bound is conservative.

First, the strong and weak adversaries yield identical empirical thresholds across all configurations. At these parameters, the binding constraint is the basin boundary rather than the adversary’s strategy: the model either recovers from the perturbation or it does not, regardless of how the perturbation is chosen.

Second, the ordering ρβ∗<ρ^∗<ρasymp∗\rho^{*}_{\beta}<\hat{\rho}^{*}<\rho^{*}_{\mathrm{asymp}} holds uniformly. The asymptotic prediction overestimates robustness because it uses the expected β\beta scaling rather than the realized (and higher) β\beta. The β\beta-tightened prediction is conservative because the theoretical analysis applies a worst-case contraction argument that does not exploit the full geometry of the energy landscape.

Third, the bound tightens at larger NN: the ratio ρ^∗/ρβ∗\hat{\rho}^{*}/\rho^{*}_{\beta} decreases from approximately 2 at N=500N=500 to approximately 1.4 at N=1000N=1000, consistent with our bounds being asymptotically tight.

The full ρ\rho-curve for the (N=500,α=0.005)(N=500,\alpha=0.005) configuration is shown in Table 6. The phase transition is sharp: success drops from 100% at ρ=0.12\rho=0.12 to 0% at ρ=0.19\rho=0.19, spanning only 7 percentage points.

B.3 Experiment 3: Capacity Scaling

We measure pmaxp_{\max}, the maximum number of patterns reliably storable, as a function of NN, and fit the power law pmax∼Nδp_{\max}\sim N^{\delta}.

Setup.

For each N∈{100,150,200,300,400,500}N\in\{100,150,200,300,400,500\}, we use binary search over pp to find pmaxp_{\max}: the largest pp at which at least 95% of 40 trials converge from 15% corruption within 60 sweeps. The effective loading αeff=pmax/Nn−1\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}=p_{\max}/N^{n-1} is also reported.

Results.

Table 7 shows the results. A power-law fit yields pmax∼0.016⋅N2.23p_{\max}\sim 0.016\cdot N^{2.23} with R2=0.9994R^{2}=0.9994. The exponent δ=2.23\delta=2.23 is close to the predicted n−1=2n-1=2; the slight excess reflects β\beta-concentration at large NN (the effective αeff\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}} increases monotonically from 0.045 to 0.068, indicating that the constant prefactor improves with NN).

The effective loading αeff≈0.068\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx 0.068 at N=500N=500 is well below the Mimura et al. capacity threshold, which in our normalization is αc=αc,3′/n≈0.266/3≈0.089\alpha_{c}=\alpha^{\prime}_{c,3}/n\approx 0.266/3\approx 0.089. This gap reflects three sources of conservatism in our setup: we require 95% success rather than merely positive overlap, use 15% corruption rather than an infinitesimal amount, and provide worst-case rather than typical-case guarantees.

B.4 Experiment 4: Comparison with Mimura et al.

We compare our results to Mimura et al. (2025) along two axes: update rule (parallel vs. asynchronous) and pattern structure (random vs. adversarially correlated).

B.4.1 Part A: Parallel vs. Asynchronous Updates

Mimura et al. analyze parallel (synchronous) updates, while our theory uses asynchronous updates. We compare both at N=500N=500 across five Mimura loading levels α3′∈{0.10,0.15,0.20,0.25,0.30}\alpha^{\prime}_{3}\in\{0.10,0.15,0.20,0.25,0.30\} (where α3′=n​p/Nn−1\alpha^{\prime}_{3}=np/N^{n-1} in Mimura’s normalization, so p=⌊α3′⋅Nn−1/n⌋p=\lfloor\alpha^{\prime}_{3}\cdot N^{n-1}/n\rfloor). Initial overlaps m0∈{0.3,0.5,0.7}m_{0}\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7\} are used, with 50 trials per configuration.

Table 8 reports success rates and mean convergence times (for successful trials only).

Asynchronous updates yield higher success rates: at α3′=0.15\alpha^{\prime}_{3}=0.15, m0=0.5m_{0}=0.5, async achieves 74% vs. parallel’s 32%. When both succeed, async also converges faster: at that configuration, async takes 5.4 sweeps vs. parallel’s 8.4. This reflects the oscillation phenomenon noted in (Mimura et al., 2025, Fig. 1): parallel updates can overshoot the fixed point, while async updates with random-permutation scheduling provide implicit damping.

B.4.2 Part B: Random vs. Adversarial Patterns

Our worst-case theory applies to arbitrary patterns (provided β<1/(n−1)\beta<1/(n-1)), while Mimura et al.’s analysis assumes i.i.d. random patterns. We quantify this gap by comparing retrieval under random patterns against adversarially correlated patterns.

Adversarial pattern construction.

Starting from a random pattern set, for the first ⌊p/3⌋\lfloor p/3\rfloor patterns, each neuron has a 25% probability of being copied from pattern ξ1\xi^{1}, injecting controlled inter-pattern correlations. This elevates β\beta from approximately 0.22 (random) to approximately 0.37 (adversarial).

Results at N=500N=500 across nine loading levels are shown in Table 9.

Random patterns achieve 100% retrieval across all tested loading levels (up to α=0.05\alpha=0.05). Adversarial patterns transition sharply from 98% success at α=0.002\alpha=0.002 to 0% at α=0.01\alpha=0.01. The adversarial β\beta values (approximately 0.37) are well above the random values (approximately 0.24) but still below 1/(n−1)=0.51/(n-1)=0.5, so the failure is driven by the interaction between elevated β\beta and the loading-dependent noise rather than by outright violation of the fundamental separation condition.

These results quantify the gap between Mimura et al.’s typical-case regime, where random patterns concentrate near their expected overlap, and our worst-case framework, which must account for adversarial correlations.

B.5 Experiment 5: MNIST and CIFAR-10

As a supplementary demonstration, we test retrieval on binarized real-world images. Patterns are binarized to ±1\pm 1 via per-image median thresholding. This experiment intentionally violates the random-pattern regime in which Proposition 10 verifies Assumptions 1 and 9; our theoretical guarantees do not apply. The purpose is to characterize practical behavior outside the theoretical regime.

Pattern statistics.

MNIST (784 dimensions, 70 000 images): the mean absolute inter-pattern overlap is |⟨ξμ,ξν⟩|/N=0.998|\langle\xi^{\mu},\xi^{\nu}\rangle|/N=0.998, with maximum 1.000. For comparison, random ±1\pm 1 patterns of the same dimension would have mean overlap approximately 1/784≈0.0361/\sqrt{784}\approx 0.036. The extreme correlation arises because median-thresholded MNIST digits are nearly identical in their binary representation: most pixels fall on the same side of the median.

CIFAR-10 (1024 dimensions, 50 000 images after grayscale conversion): mean absolute overlap is 0.158, maximum 0.848, compared to the random baseline of approximately 0.031. The correlations are elevated (roughly 5×5\times the random baseline) but far below MNIST.

Results.

Table 10 summarizes retrieval performance.

MNIST.

The model achieves 100% retrieval at all tested configurations, including p=1000p=1000 patterns at 45% corruption. This does not indicate high capacity in the usual sense: β=1.000\beta=1.000 means the theoretical condition β<1/(n−1)=0.5\beta<1/(n-1)=0.5 is violated maximally. The extreme inter-pattern correlation means that binarized MNIST digits are near-duplicates, and the cubic energy landscape has very deep basins even when patterns are not well-separated. This result underscores that our theory provides a sufficient condition for retrieval; the system can succeed even when the condition is violated, through mechanisms not captured by the worst-case analysis.

CIFAR-10.

At p=10p=10 (β=0.410<0.5\beta=0.410<0.5), the theoretical condition is satisfied and retrieval is near-perfect (97–100%). As pp increases, β\beta crosses the theoretical threshold: β=0.668\beta=0.668 at p=50p=50, β=0.779\beta=0.779 at p=100p=100, reaching β=0.900\beta=0.900 at p=1000p=1000. The degradation is smooth: at p=50p=50 success ranges from 57–93% (practical utility despite β>0.5\beta>0.5); at p=100p=100 from 15–53% (with the model often converging to a nearby spurious attractor); at p=200p=200 from 0–18% (near failure); and at p≥500p\geq 500 success is effectively 0%.

The success rate is nearly independent of noise level at moderate pp: at p=100p=100, success is 53% at both 10% and 30% corruption. The binding constraint is not the initial distance from the attractor but whether the target pattern is a stable fixed point given the β\beta level. Once β\beta is high enough to destabilize the target, reducing the initial noise does not help.

B.6 Summary of Findings

All five experiments validate the theoretical predictions. The O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) convergence bound holds with moderate constants, and β\beta-concentration at larger NN tightens the bound empirically. The basin of attraction shrinks monotonically with loading, the adversarial threshold is uniformly below the empirical recovery threshold (improving toward it as NN grows), and the capacity exponent of N2.23N^{2.23} matches the predicted Θ⁡(Nn−1)\Theta(N^{n-1}) scaling. Asynchronous updates consistently outperform parallel updates, and adversarially correlated patterns degrade performance sharply relative to random ones. On real data, CIFAR-10 confirms that β\beta rather than noise level governs capacity breakdown, while MNIST’s universal retrieval illustrates that the separation condition is sufficient but not necessary.
